articles.title: Deadlock in New Zealand's election leaves Opportunity the decider
articles.description: The final vote count in New Zealand’s election showed neither the right-wing incumbents nor the left-wing opposition bloc won enough seats in Parliament to form a majority government. The result published Friday left the prospect of lengthy negotiations to break the deadlock. The election Nov. 7 was the tightest in years and left the conservative bloc, led by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon, with a collective 65 seats. The left-wing opposition, led by Labour’s Chris Hipkins, won 58 seats in the 130-seat Parliament, with 66 needed for a majority government. The figures leave a new entrant to parliament, the centrist Opportunity party that won seven seats, as the deciders of the next government.

articles.title: WHO Director-General's opening remarks at joint media briefing with the Ministry of Public Health, Haiti – 25 November 2026
articles.description: Minister Sinal, Minister Forbin, Members of the ambassadors, my colleagues from the UN, press, and friends, Good afternoon, and thank you for joining us today. First, I would like to sincerely thank Minister Sinal and the Government of Haiti for their warm welcome and for the constructive discussions we have had during my visit. It has given me the chance to reaffirm WHO/PAHO's solidarity with Haiti and its people, including my personal commitment for WHO to do all in its power to support the country. During my visit earlier today to Hôpital Universitaire La Paix here in the capital, Port-au-Prince, I saw first-hand the strain the facility and its staff are working under, and the patients and families waiting for care. It moved me. Haiti's health system is under serious strain from the high volume of patients and the influx of trauma cases. Armed violence, widespread displacement and disease outbreaks add to the pressure on an already fragile system. In 2026, an estimated 4.9 million people need health assistance. Behind every number is a mother, a child, a family. Health facilities have been forced to close, and too many families are unable to access even the most basic health services. As you know, H.U.P. is the last major public referral hospital still operating in Port-au-Prince, a city where only 38% of health facilities are fully functional. Across Haiti, a country of more than 11 million people, only a quarter (24.5%) of health facilities are fully functioning. Since January of this year, with support from WHO/PAHO, H.U.P. has managed to treat more than 19 575 emergency patients, including 291 victims of gunshot wounds, perform 3086 surgeries, and handle 1442 high-risk deliveries. From my heart, I thank the brave, committed and talented health workers who provide a lifeline for the people of Port-au-Prince. They are working day and night in one of the most challenging humanitarian and health crises globally, and they continue to show great courage and dedication. I was proud to meet some of them earlier today. I also want to recognize the leadership of Minister Sinal and the Ministry of Public Health and Population in sustaining essential health services under difficult circumstances. Earlier today, I met with the Prime Minister. I left that meeting encouraged and inspired by what the government is doing with the limited resources it has, especially with maternal and child health at the center. His message to the international community was, I quote: “We will do our best, and you support us based on the priorities we set for our country.” It is a message we should listen to. Through our Regional Office for the Americas, PAHO, WHO is working closely with the Ministry and our partners to support emergency medical care, respond to outbreaks, strengthen disease surveillance and immunization, and maintain access to essential medicines and medical supplies. Even so, Haiti’s Ministry of Public Health and Population has moved forward with the introduction of the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine to help prevent cervical cancer. Our discussions have reaffirmed three shared priorities. First, protecting health workers, patients and health facilities. Second, ensuring safe and sustained access to essential health services. And third, strengthening Haiti's health system to respond not only to today's emergencies, but also to tomorrow's challenges. Health is not only a humanitarian priority. Health is a fundamental human right, and a foundation for peace, stability and sustainable development. These efforts require strong national leadership, sustained international solidarity and predictable financing. I want to thank our partners for their continued support, which is helping to save lives every day. But the needs remain significant. The people of Haiti need our support today, and our partnership in the years ahead. They are not alone. Minister Sinal, You can count on WHO and PAHO's continued solidarity, commitment and support. I can say this on behalf of the whole UN family. We stand with you, and with the people of Haiti. Thank you. Merci. Mèsi anpil.
